about: The words of the cards of Data/encounters/danes_norway_793.json (the region danes_norway: Ripa, Sliesthorp, Reric, Hleidr, Ahus, Skiringssal, Ogvaldsnes), with a picture line for each card (art.<card id>) and five news items (danes_norway.news.*: one of them, thorleif_drowned, is false on purpose). Written 7 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Many first greetings keep the people's own lines from the places files, so that a person sounds the same on a card as in the port. Riddles said aloud are our own plain renderings of Heidreks gatur (the riddles of Gestumblindi) and of Vafthruthnismal 26; the one sentence quoted from a translation is Thorir Sel's boast, 'When we took the sail from him he wept' (Heimskringla, Saint Olaf's saga 124, tr. S. Laing 1844).

entries.text: Whose guest
A broad man with a square grey beard has walked down the sand before your keel has touched it. He looks at the boat first, then at you, and waits.

A low sand bank on a brown river at morning: a broad Dane in a brown tunic and a cloak pinned at the right shoulder stands with his thumbs in his belt before a small Frisian boat just grounding; behind him a row of booths with their backs to the wind.
A Frisian boat, and small. Good. Small boats pay what they owe. Whose guest are you on this bank? If nobody's, say so now.
You came back over the flats and did not drown. My youngest owes me an ounce. He bet on the flats.
My guest is here. Tell me what Dorestat says, and I will tell you what it should have said.
Last time you were nobody's guest. Nobody answered for you, and nobody had to. It is a cold way to trade.
Your gift was a fair one. I showed it at the fire. That is what a gift is for.
With us a stranger has no peace until a man of the place stands for him. I stand for mine. So when you cheat, cheat somewhere else.
The herds are coming down from the heath. You will smell the market before you see it.
King's men are on the bank asking each skipper whose man he is. If they ask you, you are mine. Say it before they finish asking.
Give the guest's gift and take his hand (6 d of silver, weighed)
Sit at the bench end, as before
Ask for his youngest to teach you the channels over the flats (12 d)
Say you are your own man here
Silver has one face
A thin man with burn-scarred forearms is tapping a brooch on a block, a quick double tap, like a wagtail. Beside him lie a folding scale in a bronze case and a row of small lead weights.

A turf-walled booth with broken clay moulds heaped by the door: a thin goldsmith in a leather apron holds up a small folding scale, a penny in one pan and a lead weight in the other; charcoal glow, a Frisian's hand held out in the foreground.
Put it on the scale. No, not the coin's face to me. I do not know your king. Silver has one face, and it is the inside.
The Frisian with the pennies. Still counting them? Count this: you were paid a tenth short at the last booth, and you smiled.
Your king has made a new penny, they say, and the old ones are dead. Not here. Dead coin weighs what it weighed.
Three ounces for a scale that folds and a set of my weights. I show you the nick and the bend for nothing. After that no man north of the Eider cheats you twice.
While you think: who walks hard paths, kisses fast, has two mouths and treads on nothing but gold? I am holding him.
You have him. I can see it. Say it, then, and I will stop hitting things for a moment out of respect.
Buy the scale and the weights, and learn the nick (48 d)
Buy his riddle to take away (4 d)
Tell him who treads on nothing but gold
Let him weigh your pennies, and keep your purse shut
Leaves by the handful
On the goldsmith's block lies a strip of gilt knotwork with rivet holes in it. He is wrapping a brooch mould in a square of pale calfskin, and the calfskin has a painted beast on it.

A goldsmith's booth at dusk: on the block a strip of gilt knotwork with rivet holes, and under the smith's burn-scarred hand a painted calfskin leaf with a blue beast, half wrapped round a clay mould.
See this? Gold, off two boards. A north-way crew sold it me after midsummer. Good work. I have copied the knot already.
Between the boards were calfskins with black marks and painted beasts. I wrap moulds in them. They take the heat well. Nine left.
The crew had a boy who tallied their cargo on a stick, faster than the steersman. Cropped head. They would not sell him. I asked.
Their chief winters on the sound where the ships go north. Red beard, laughs first. I still owe him the last ounce. He has not forgotten. Nor have I.
You have been taught what a book is. Nine leaves of a gospel are wrapping brooch moulds here, for the price of a string of beads.
Buy the nine leaves (12 d)
Leave the skins, and ask the chief's name and where the sound is
A word at the well
Beside the old well an ale-wife keeps a bench under an awning. Everyone who needs water comes here, so everyone who has news leaves some. She is already pouring.

A square oak-lined well with a pole and a stave bucket, the ground trodden to paste: a strong fair woman in a blue strap dress with a string of glass beads pours from a ladle at a bench under a wadmal awning; boatmen on the bench, a cask-lined second well behind.
New face, Frisian boat, four men. Sit. Where from, what in the hold, and who is your host? Drink first. You can lie to me after.
You sat there last time and paid for three cups because you could not count our weights. I kept the difference. Here it is.
A woman offered two ounces for a Frankish pot with a crack in it. No Frisian has come with pots since the ice went. I say it once.
Malt. Before Yule a Northman pays what you ask for malt. After Yule he haggles. Remember who told you.
You are a man short. There is one on my bench whose crew went north without him. He was not drowned. Drowned men get talked about.
My sister keeps the alehouse at the Heaths. If you go there, say Tola is well and the carters are slow. She will know both already.
I do not want a wage from you. I want a tenth part in a cargo, and my name said when it is sold. Think about it while you drink.
Stand the bench a round and send her word of the pots south (2 d)
Take the hand she names (4 d to bind him)
Give her a tenth part in this cargo
Drink your cup and tell her as little as you can
Blue for Toki
A stooped man with singed eyebrows turns a blob of blue glass on an iron rod over a clay hearth no bigger than a shield. The floor round him glitters with beads that went wrong.

An open-sided booth with a small clay hearth: an old stooped bead-maker with singed eyebrows turns a drop of blue glass on an iron rod; the floor glitters with failed beads; antler splinters drift in from the comb-maker's side; a string of bright beads round his wrist.
Beads. Blue, yellow, striped, eyed. Each one turned by hand, which is why they cost more and why nobody wants them. What have you brought me? Say glass.
The Frisian. Did you bring blue? No? Then sit and watch a man work for nothing. It is free.
A Gute laid out eastern beads ten days ago, thin as peas. A string for what I ask for five. The women bought them and smiled at me kindly.
You took my order. I told the hearth. The hearth does not believe in Frisians either.
That sack. That is not grain. Open it. Slowly. I am an old man.
There is a Frisian drilling amber among the Wends who says I keep the best Rhine glass and send on the rest. He is right. Tell him so. It will annoy him.
Sell him two sacks of raw glass, for beads and weighed silver
Take his order for blue glass from the Rhine
Buy a string of his best at the maker's price (8 d)
Watch him turn a bead, and go
The cattle ground
Above the last plot the river spreads thin over gravel. A carter sits on his cart tail by the hurdles with a hazel goad across his knees, looking at his oxen as if they might say something.

A wide trampled ground fenced with hurdles beside a gravel ford: small dun cattle steaming, a heavy-shouldered carter in a wool hood on the tail of an ox cart, a notched stick behind his ear, a dog barking at nothing; grey autumn light.
Mind the dung, it is the oldest thing in this market. You want goods taken inland, or cattle brought out? I do both. Slowly.
The Frisian. My oxen remember your casks. They did not like them. Wine sloshes. It upsets an ox.
The herds are down from the heath and fat. Buy hides before the frost, or wait till spring and buy them thin.
Sit on the cart tail. Four go, four hang, two show the way, two keep off dogs, one drags dirty behind. No hurry. The oxen have not guessed it either.
You have it. I can tell by how you look at my beasts. Say it, then.
I carried wood at the king's hall on Zealand as a boy. The steward there taught me the tally. He never hurried in his life, and I took after him.
Buy two bundles of hides off the drovers through him (24 d)
Take the riddle away with you
Give him the answer
Wish him good pasture and walk on
Whose man
A man in a red cloak has laid his hand on your stem, as a friend might. Behind him carts of hard bread and coiled rope are going down to the water.

The market bank on a grey morning: a king's man in a red cloak with one hand on the stem of a small Frisian boat; behind him ox carts of bread and coiled rope going down to the water, and a broad Dane standing a little way off with his arms folded.
A Frisian keel. Small. Whose man are you this summer, friend? I ask as a friend.
The king is buying rope, tar and bread that keeps. He pays in weighed silver and does not haggle. He has not the time.
The ships go east this summer, against the Wends. That is no secret. Where they go after is not mine to say.
Your coast owes the king a hundred pounds of silver, I hear. I should be glad to know the Frisian who paid early.
Your host has come down the bank and stands a little behind you, saying nothing, where the king's man can see him.
Say you are your host's guest, and nobody's man
Sell him two coils of rope and two barrels of tar at his price
Sell him six sacks of ship's bread
Say you are nobody's man but your own
Grain over the flats
The ale-wife has looked in your hold before you have sat down. On the plots a Danish woman is already weighing out cut silver, and nobody is looking toward the south.

First light on the market bank: sacks of rye being handed from a small Frisian boat up the sand, a Danish woman weighing cut silver on a folding scale, an ale-wife with her arms folded, and nobody looking toward the south.
What is in the hold? Do not sit down first. Barley is twice its price here, and rye is whatever you dare ask.
Your king has forbidden this, I hear. No food out of his realm in a hungry year. He has not forbidden it here. He has not been asked.
The corn Frisian. I say it kindly. Everyone here says it kindly.
On the Frisian coast the poor are at the church doors this year. Here a sack of rye is worth a good knife.
Sell four sacks of rye at the bank's price
Sell four sacks of barley
Say the grain is spoken for at home
A dead guest
West of the last booth the sand rises a little and nobody builds. A pyre is stacked there, unlit. Your host is waiting beside it with something to ask you.

A low sandy rise of small mounds and old pyre patches beside a market: an unlit pyre of split logs, a shrouded shape on a plank, a broad Dane with his cloak pulled close, and a Frisian crew standing a few paces off with their caps in their hands.
A Frisian off the big ship died in my neighbour's house last night. Fever. His skipper went out on the tide and left two ounces and no word.
A guest who dies is still a guest. I will not have him lie about. What do your people do with their dead? Tell me, and I will see it done, or near it.
The wood is stacked in case you have no better answer. Larks are singing over the heather, and behind you the market goes on.
Your steersman has taken off his cap. The grey Northman is looking at the pyre as a man looks at a well-built boat.
Bury him in the sand, head to the west, and say over him what you remember
Let the market burn him with honour, as it would its own
Pay for his grave ale, so the bank drinks to a stranger (10 d)
The short ell
A farmer from inland has come down to the plots with a folded bolt of your cloth under his arm and three neighbours behind him. Your host has been sent for.

The plots at midday: a lean Jutland farmer holds a length of blue cloth stretched along his forearm, three neighbours watching; a broad host stands between him and a Frisian merchant; on a post hangs a plain heavy arm ring.
This Frisian sold me cloth at midsummer. Eight ells, he said. I have laid it on my own arm since. Seven and a hand.
My arm is longer than his. That is where the hand went. But he has said it before witnesses, so it must be answered before witnesses.
The custom is the ring, in front of the bank. A man lays his hand on it and says the thing was so. Then it was so, and nobody speaks of it again.
He is my guest. If he will not swear, I may. I would rather not. An oath is a thing a man has only so many of.
Lay your hand on the ring and swear the cloth was full measure
Offer to swear by your own God, with your hand on your boat's stem
Ask your host to swear for his guest
Give the man his hand of cloth back in silver (6 d)
Four posts and a sea chest

On the south bank, facing the market across the river, four corner posts stand on a staked plot with a sea chest between them. A wiry young priest in a much-darned habit is beating a board with a stick, softly.

A staked plot by a river in the rain: four corner posts, a sea chest for an altar, a wiry tonsured priest in a darned black habit kilted out of the mud holding a clapper board; across the water the booths of a market and faces turned to look.
God's welcome. This is the church at Ripa. I grant you it needs walls. I say Mass on a sea chest. In wet weather, under it.
You came back. That doubles my congregation of Frisians. Mass is at first light. I beat a board, softly, so the market can pretend not to hear.
The king gave the ground and leave for a priest to live on it. He did not say live well. I want oak, nails and a man who can cut reed.
You have something wrapped in a cloak, and you are holding it as a layman holds a thing he knows he should not.
Bishop Anskar died at Bremen, the day after Candlemas. I said the Mass. Now tell me: who remembers there is a priest at Ripa?
It is a fast day. I would offer you fish, but the market has bought it all to spite me. There is bread.
Give two loads of oak for the walls
Take his order for oak
Give him the altar cup from the Vik
Hear his Mass at the sea chest
Set down on the south bank
The king's men have staked the plot on the south bank: four hazel rods and a cord. Across the river the whole market has found work to do at the water's edge.

A small Frisian boat nosed into the south bank of a river: a young priest steps over the side holding a cross, two boatmen lifting a sea chest after him; four hazel rods and a cord mark a bare plot; across the water a market crowd pretending not to watch.
So. Four rods. I have had smaller cells and worse neighbours. Help me up the bank with the chest. It is the altar now, and I should not drop it on the first day.
The fare I cannot pay. The bishop said you would be paid in the reckoning that matters. He says that to everyone. He also gave me this for you.
Stay a day and set his four corner posts with your crew
Carry the chest up, take the bishop's gift, and catch the ebb
The writ at the church door
A tall, well-fed bishop in a cloak of good English cloth stands at the church door with a clerk beside him. Near by a moneyer's man sweeps new pennies into a wooden bowl like peas.

A timber church by a river, its door open: a tall fair-bearded bishop in a gold-bordered cloak with a staff headed in walrus ivory, a clerk unrolling a parchment beside him, merchants and farmers listening; to one side a moneyer's bench with a bowl of new pennies.
You are welcome in Ripa. The king's peace covers you from the outer sand to the ford. Past the ford my own covers you, which is nearly as good.
The house from the Rhine mouths. Your father's father traded on this bank before there was a church to tithe him. I have it from the old women.
The king's word is read at this door. One peace on both shores of the sea. A law you have heard is harder to break by accident.
The king was at Rome at Easter and bargained with the emperor over merchants' tolls on the road. A king who haggles for traders. Mark it.
Men are home from England with more pennies than they can spend. My moneyer weighs them and weeps: good silver, and every one with the wrong king.
Dine with me. It is a fast day, so it will be fish, but it will be a great deal of fish.
Stand at the church door and hear the writ read
Dine with the bishop, and hear what was done at Rome
Give to the church of Ripa (10 d)
The landing gift
A spare man with a tally stick in his belt is waiting where the brook has cut a channel in the sand. He watches where you drive your stake, and says nothing until it is in.

A still brown inner water ringed with reeds, small boats on rollers and a short timber jetty: a spare grey Dane with a tally stick in his belt stands on the strand watching a Frisian crew drive a mooring stake; thatch and smoke on a green slope behind.
You lie where the brook has cut the sand, like everyone. I speak for this strand until somebody greater says he does. A gift is usual.
The small boat from the river. Your stake hole is still in the shallows. Nobody used it. I would have heard.
Last time you gave nothing and nothing happened to you. That is not the same as being safe.
The king is on the heath with every horse in the kingdom. Lie close in. His men buy bread at any price and take fodder at none.
There is a wall now, and one gate in it, and I am the man with the stick. A cart for the western river pays going out. So the king says.
Every guest of the king owes days on the wall, or the price of a man's days. Your notch is cut already. I cut it when I saw your sail.
The people on the strand with bundles are the Wends' merchants. The king brought them. They are counting what they carried. It does not take long.
Give the landing gift (4 d of silver, weighed)
Pay the price of your crew's days on the wall (60 d)
Say you lodge with Gunnhild, and she answers for you
Give nothing, and see to your boat
Gunnhild's stick

A long house of wattle and reed thatch, the door on the lee side. Above the ale vat a row of notched sticks is stuck in the wall, one for each guest who has not paid. A broad woman is looking for yours.

The inside of a long thatched house by firelight: benches along both walls, sea chests under them, a row of notched tally sticks stuck in the wall above an ale vat; a broad woman with keys and a knife at her belt holds one stick up to the fire.
Ale is brewed, the bench is dry, the fire is yours until you fall asleep at it. I am Gunnhild. Who answers for you here?
I kept your stick. Three notches unpaid, or two. I forget in your favour once and never twice.
A man with no host here is driftwood. Anyone may pick him up. Say you lodge with me and they will leave you be.
There are Saxons in my back room who would not be moved into Francia. They pay in work. They jump when a horse passes.
Asulf's men drink here, and they talk. Ask me about the island boys, and I tell you for nothing what Asulf would charge a blade for.
As I told you: the island boys went east with a Svea called Holmfast, of Birka, who weighs everything three times. Asulf knows who told you. He is polite about it.
My Thorgar is in one of the two hundred ships. If you were on the Frisian coast this summer, do not tell me what you saw. Tell me he was not in it.
My sister at Ripa sends word by the carters. It comes a month old and all of it true, which is the worst kind.
Lodge the crew with her and pay your notches (6 d)
Ask what Asulf's men said about the island boys
Give her two sacks of malt for the house
Drink one cup and sleep aboard
A fast day at the long fire
A pig is turning over the long fire in the alehouse, and the fat spits. By your crew's reckoning it is a fast day. They are sitting in a row, not eating, and being looked at.

A long fire down the middle of a thatched house, a pig on a spit over it: four Frisian boatmen sit in a row on the bench with their hands on their knees, looking at the meat; a broad ale-wife with a ladle and an old ferryman with a basket of eels look at them.
Your men sit like herons and look at my pork as if it had insulted them. Is it the meat or the price?
They are fasting. It is a thing their god asks. On some days he likes them hungry. Ours only asks that on a lee shore.
Fish I have not. Hallbjorn has eels, and opinions about what eels are worth to a man whose god is watching.
The grey Northman has taken a rib and is eating it slowly, looking at nobody.
Buy the ferryman's eels for the crew (3 d)
Have the men eat bread and ale, and keep the day
Eat the pork with the house, and say nothing of days
Double, on the scale
Two men have been watching your boat since she touched the sand: a young Dane with a good sword belt and no sword in it, and a stout man tapping his boot with a hazel switch.

A northern market's booths: a young Danish warrior with an empty sword belt and a stout dealer in a grey cloak with a hazel switch stand either side of a Frisian merchant; a folding scale hangs from the dealer's hand; furs and amber on the boards behind.
You are from the river where the good iron is made. I do not ask what is under your ballast. I say what it would weigh in silver if it were there.
A blade with the smith's name in it: double its river price, on the scale, today. My lord has many ships and not enough edges.
He pays in silver. I pay in people, who are worth more further on. Think which you would rather carry past your king's toll.
Since the emperor's order no arms may leave his realm. Both men know it. It is why the price is double.
In the west the price of arming Northmen is now a man's life. Here it is still double, on the scale.
The grey Northman has walked off to look at the water. He will not stand near the man with the hazel switch.
Sell the Dane two swords for double, in weighed silver
Sell him two bare blades
Sell the dealer a sword for one of his lot
Say you carry cloth, and remember both faces
A man who remembers every sale

A fenced yard above the strand with a roof along one side. A row of notched sticks hangs on a peg by the gate, one for each ship that sold here this year. The dealer takes one down without being asked.

A fenced pen at dusk: a stout man in a grey cloak with a silver ring pin holds a notched stick up to the last light, a row of sticks on a peg behind him; on a bench a sealskin, two cups and a bell without a tongue; people sitting in rows under a lean-to roof.
You are from the river. I am Asulf. I buy and sell people, and I pay in silver by weight. Sit, if that does not offend you.
The Frisian with the small boat. You came back, so I did not cheat you, or you did not notice. Either is good for trade.
The island lot. Church boys, soft hands. I have the stick here. Where they went has a price, and I name it once: one Frankish blade.
Or carry this stick to Thorleif on the Kormt sound. It says what he owes me and nothing else. Do that, and I tell it as one trader to another.
One more came through three summers after the rest. He could tally. He fetched more than the other three together. That much I tell you for nothing.
The grey Northman waits outside the fence, with his back to it.
Pay his price: one sword
Take his tally stick for Thorleif
Tell him the stick is in Thorleif's hand
Thank him, and ask in the alehouse instead
Four hazel rods and a king
On a plot paced out with a knotted rope, short end to the water, a wide-faced man in a fur-edged cap sits on a bundle beside four hazel rods. There is bread on a cloth in front of him.

A narrow plot by a brook marked by four hazel rods, raw earth and a half-built wattle house: a wide-faced Wend in a fur-edged cap, a ring of twisted silver wire at his temple, sits on a bundle with bread on a cloth before him; behind, a long earth bank with men digging.
You are from the west. I had a booth at Reric. Now I have four hazel rods and a king. Sit. There is still bread. A Wend with no bread for a guest is dead.
The Frisian who kept faith. Sit by me. I have told the others your name, and they have told me it is hard to say.
I ask one thing of every ship: does she go back along that coast? My wife's brother holds a fort inland. He does not know which of us lives.
You have my tally still. Wends lie on the river bank in Skane, under the comb-makers' town. Any of them will carry it home.
The king takes his due at the gate now, and again at the far end of the road. At Reric I paid one Dane. Here I pay two and am called fortunate.
They say the king is dead, by one of his own. I did not drink to it. I sat very still, like a man who has learned something about kings.
Take his tally for his kin on the Wendish shore
Buy two cakes of wax at his own price (64 d)
Eat his bread and tell him what the west says
Fodder, ale and bread
The heath south of the houses is covered: striped tents, horse lines out to the edge of sight, shields on spear racks. A king's man and the ale-wife reach your boat at the same moment.

A wide heath covered with striped wool tents and horse lines to the horizon, a high seat carried out of a ship in an open space; in the foreground a king's man with a scale and a broad ale-wife both with a hand on the same sack in a small Frisian boat.
The king lies on the heath with every horseman he owns. My vat is empty by noon. If that is malt in your boat, I will fight his man for it.
The king's horses eat and the king's men drink. I buy grain, malt and bread by weight of silver, and I do not ask where it grew.
One thing I do ask. What do the emperor's horsemen eat this year, on your side of the river? The king likes to know. Answer that one carefully.
Sell Gunnhild four sacks of malt
Sell the king's man four sacks of rye
Tell him plainly what you saw on the emperor's road
Say you are a river man and know only river prices
Rye for a knife
Before you have made fast, three women from the booths are standing at the brook mouth with scales in their hands, and Gunnhild in front of them.

A strand of sand and mussel shell: three women with folding scales and a broad ale-wife in front of them stand at the water's edge facing a small Frisian boat with sacks under her deck boards; thin smoke over the thatch behind.
Hunger in the south, they say, and your emperor has shut his barns with a law. Here a sack of rye is worth a good knife. I made neither rule.
The people behind my hanging eat too, and they are his own Saxons. Tell your emperor that, when he asks where his rye went.
You brought corn last time. The whole strand knows your sail now. That is good for you here. I would not shout it at home.
Sell four sacks of rye on the strand
Sell four sacks of barley
Say the grain is spoken for at home
Cloth with the seal still on it

A booth by the brook has blue cloth on the board with a lead seal still on the selvage. You know the seal. It is Dorestat's. Behind the booth, under the pen's roof, somebody has said your boat's name.

A booth of poles and sailcloth by a brook: bolts of blue cloth with a small lead seal hanging from one; behind it a fenced pen where a young woman in a torn Frisian gown stands at the hurdle looking straight out; a dealer with a switch between them and the viewer.
Cloth from the river, and people from the river, both sound. The king says the fleets are not his. I say only that the goods are here.
You are from the dams. I know your boat. I am a weaver's daughter from the row behind the bank road. Tell them I am alive. I do not ask more than that.
She weaves. A hundred and twenty by weight, and I do not haggle twice. The cloth is cheaper. Nobody cries over cloth.
The king has sent word to the emperor that he took the chiefs of those fleets and killed them, and asks for Frisia in thanks.
Buy her free and carry her home (120 d)
Buy three bolts of the sealed cloth cheap (72 d)
Promise to carry her name to the dams
Boys, books and ships
A thin tonsured man in a black habit worn at the hem sits by a door with a row of boys reading from wax tablets behind him. He is counting something on his fingers when you come up.

A plain plank room by a harbour: a thin tonsured monk in a worn black habit sits by the open door; behind him a row of Danish and Wendish boys bend over wax tablets, sharing one small book; through the door, ships at a jetty.
God keep you. You came by ship, so you have news and wet feet. Sit by the door. The Danes like to see who is inside.
You again, thank God. I count the ships that come back. It is a shorter list than the ones I bless.
I buy boys out of the pens here, Danes and Wends, and teach them letters. Twelve now. They share one psalter and fight over it like dogs over a bone.
I set out for the Svear with nearly forty books. Sea robbers took the ship and I arrived on foot with none. Someone has them. Books are not eaten.
The king has given us a roof by the harbour. Merchants from your river hear Mass openly now. Others take the sign of the cross and wait for their deathbed.
The count has nailed our door shut and says the gods are angry. I am patient. Counts are put out more often than doors.
You are carrying a book. I can tell by how the crew steps round the chest.
Give a book to his school
Sell him a book at a fair price (240 d)
Take his order for calfskin for the school
Tell him where you have seen leaves sold for scraping
A priest for Ripa
By the church door a greying bishop in a plain cloak is standing beside a wiry young priest, a sea chest, and a board with a stick tied to it. Both of them are looking at your boat.

A small plank church by a harbour with an empty oak frame beside its door: a greying bishop in a plain cloak, a wiry young priest with a wooden cross on a cord, a sea chest and a clapper board at their feet; a small Frisian boat at the jetty behind.
The young king has given ground at Ripa for a second church. I have the ground and a priest. I have not a ship, and the heath road is long for a man carrying an altar.
I am the priest. Liudlef. I was a boy in the pen here once. The bishop bought me for letters. This is the debt I am paying, and I mean to pay it cheerfully.
He has a sea chest, a clapper board and a cross. However you came here, you go back to the western sea. Set him down at Ripa, on the south bank. He cannot pay. I can, a little.
Take the priest, his chest and his board aboard for Ripa
Take him for a fare, paid now (10 d)
Say the flats are no place for a sea chest
More than a man can drink
On the plank street by the moneyer's bench a young man in a cloak too new for him is pouring pennies from one hand to the other and looking at your cargo.

A plank street running down to jetties in autumn: a young Dane in a bright new cloak pours silver pennies from hand to hand; beside him a moneyer astride a block with a die and a small scale; a rampart of turf behind the houses.
I was in England with the fleet. They paid us to go away. So we went away, and here I am with more pennies than a man can drink.
I want what a man with silver should have. Wine from the south. A cup that is glass. Have you either? Name the count. I have stopped weighing.
His pennies have the English king's head on, every one. Good silver. I weigh them, and then I count them, and both come out the same. At home that is the law. Here it is new.
Ten thousand pounds, they say, the first time. The English king thinks he has bought peace. He has bought a second visit.
King Cnut holds both shores now, and the pennies of both go across one bench.
Sell him two casks of Rhenish wine for pennies by count
Sell him a crate of glass
Drink with him and hear how the tribute was shared
Cups for the pot
In the lean-to against the goldsmith's house the boy is already blowing up the charcoal. The moneyer has the four cups in a row on his block and is turning the fourth in his hands.

A lean-to open at the front: a moneyer astride a block holds a silver cup worked with beasts up to the light, three plainer cups in a row before him, a boy at a small bellows, a crucible in the charcoal.
Four cups. Old work. One has beasts on it that I do not know. Whose they were I do not ask. I ask what they weigh.
Weight for weight, less a tenth for the pot. Or keep the one with the beasts. A thing like that is worth more whole, to the right house, and nothing at all to my fire.
Sell all four for the pot
Sell three, and keep the one with the beasts for the house
The slip under the alders
A hull stands on blocks north of the brook, half planked, her ribs not yet in. A thick-shouldered man walks round her with an axe and does not seem to measure anything.

A strip of shore black with old tar under alders: a half-planked clinker hull on blocks, thin split-oak strakes overlapping like fish scales; a thick-shouldered wright with chips in his sandy beard and a broad axe; a boy heating rivets at a small fire.
Do not lean on her, the tar is wet. I am Thormund. I build what the oak allows, and I mend what other men built.
Let me see what you did to her. Hm. The sea did half of it. The other half was you.
A Frisian hull is a tub. I say it kindly. She carries twice what mine does, and arrives when the weather has finished with her.
Order before the leaves fall and she swims at first open water. Order in spring and you get my opinion of spring orders.
The king's ships come first on my slip this summer, whether I like it or not. I am paid in the king's thanks. You may guess what they weigh.
There is a wright at the river mouth in Skane who says I build for fair weather. He mends. I build. A man who only mends has opinions.
Sell him two kegs of rivets
Take his order for iron
Have him look her over and say what she needs (2 d)
Leave him to his oak
The white street
A small sunken hut on the north-west edge, a roof on the ground with a doorway and a man working in the light of it. He saws antler into plates, ankle-deep in white shavings.

A row of sunken huts with roofs to the ground: in one doorway a comb-maker with a fine saw sits ankle-deep in white antler shavings, comb plates in a row beside him; at a yard gate two poles with a ram's hide hung between them.
Antler? No. Then you want combs, and I am the wrong man to ask about the price, because I made them.
The Frisian. Your last dozen: did the teeth hold? They hold. I ask because I like to hear it.
The man in the next hut is from the river mouth in Skane. He comes every summer and sets up beside me, and we watch each other's prices like two dogs with one bone.
The Skane men have gone home with the herring. Now the street is mine, and there is nobody to sell to. That is the joke of this trade.
Mind the floor. It is white to the ankle. One day somebody will count the offcuts and think we were rich.
That bundle is antler. Shed, by the burr. Put it down here.
Sell him two bundles of antler for combs
Buy a dozen combs at the hut's price (10 d)
Offer to carry his greeting to the comb-maker at the river mouth
Step round the shavings and go on
The ferryman's fare

A tarred four-oared boat at a stake where the inner water opens into the Slie. The ferryman sits in the stern with a small bag tied under his seat, and looks at the water as at a neighbour he has not forgiven.

A tarred ferry boat on grey water, reeds and oak wood on the far shore: a long-armed old man with white hair in a tail and a face like a dried apple rests on his oars, mouth open in mid-word; further out a dark line of logs shows above the water.
Sit in the middle and keep your feet off the bag. The fare is a cut of silver, or a thing I have not heard before.
You. I told the water you would be back. It did not answer, but it never does when it agrees.
Who are the brides that walk over the reefs and drive along the friths? White hoods. A hard bed. In calm weather they make no stir.
I have one of three sisters. A Vestfold shipman has the first, a singer among the Svear the second. Bring me all three, said together.
A grey Northman sails with you. Ask him about the low bench by the door. Then watch him talk about the weather.
There is a fence of logs across the narrows, older than my father. Kings built it. I know the gap. Strangers find it with their keels.
Pay the fare in silver and take his riddle with you (2 d)
Say the three sisters together in his boat
Hire him to take you through the gap in the log fence (4 d)
Pay the fare with what you saw on the way here
Driftwood
The Saxon you bought at Reric stands on the strand with his hands open, looking at the houses as if one of them might know him. Gunnhild has come down from her door.

The brook-mouth strand: a young Saxon with rope marks on his wrists stands with open hands beside a small Frisian boat, looking up at thatched houses; a broad ale-wife comes down the slope toward him wiping her hands on her apron.
Another one. They come up this strand like driftwood. Who answers for him? A man with no host is anybody's.
My father was a smith beyond the Elbe. I can draw a rivet and shoe a horse. I ask nobody for bread I have not worked for.
There is room behind my hanging, with his own people. Or he is your guest, and then his conduct is yours. Say which.
Answer for him yourself, and pay his first winter (20 d)
Ask Gunnhild to take him behind the hanging with the others
The king's awning
A sail is stretched over four posts at the top of the shore. Under it a lean Dane sits on a chest with a folding scale hung from a spear shaft, and two men with shields are asleep against a boat.

A long low shore of grey sand and reeds: a sail stretched over four posts, a lean Dane with a notched upper lip seated on a chest beneath it, a folding scale hanging from a spear shaft; behind him a heap of wax cakes, a quern and a bundle of marten; Wends walking past without looking.
A new boat. Lay it out on the sand, all of it. The king takes his part by weight, and I do the weighing.
You. Your goods were honest last time. Lay them out anyway. I am paid to look.
They ask why a Dane takes the due on a Wend's shore. I ask why the Wend pays it. Neither of us answers.
The king has been counting ships this winter. When a king counts ships, I would not buy a house near water.
If I were a Frisian with a sound boat I would have business elsewhere before the hay is in. I have said nothing.
You have a scale of your own now. Then we shall agree, and I shall be sorry. I liked being right alone.
Under your ballast are things the emperor's law forbids you to sell here, and this man lays every cargo out on the sand.
Lay it out and pay the king's part (5 d of silver, weighed)
Ask him to teach you the weights and the nick (12 d)
Leave the blades under the ballast and lay out the rest
Sit under the sail a while and let him talk
Dragomir's table

The largest house in its lane, with a table that is never cleared: bread, millet, smoked fish, a bowl of honey, mead in a wooden cup that goes round. A sharp-eyed woman at the end turns every guest's words into the next guest's tongue.

A house above ground among sunken huts: a laid table with bread, smoked fish, a bowl of honey and a wooden cup; a wide-faced Wend in a fur-edged cap holds up half a thin silver coin on a thong; at the table's end a thin dark-browed woman with bronze rings at her temples leans forward to speak.
A Frisian. Sit, eat first. A man who talks prices on an empty belly gets the price he deserves.
You said you would come back with the open water, and here is the water and here are you. Liuba, the good mead.
He says eat. He means it. Among us a house that sends a stranger away hungry is talked of for three winters.
Look at this. A Svea brought it. Half a coin, thin, broad, covered in writing no priest of yours could read. What would the Franks give for a bag of them?
The Svea called the makers the people of the south river. That told me nothing either. It is purer than a penny. I bit it.
I would send my eastern silver west in one boat, for a tenth of the difference. I ask no oath. To swear is halfway to forswearing. Take my hand. It has never yet been wrong.
We are given the Saxons' fields. Fields want ploughshares. Bring me iron and I will not ask what shape it was first.
Take the half coin in your hand, and say honestly that you do not know
Take his hand on it: his silver west in your boat
Buy wax and honey from his table at a guest's price (56 d)
Eat, praise the mead, and talk of weather
Three tongues and the interpreter's fourth

In the straight lanes goods are set out on the edges of roofs hardly higher than your belt, and you understand one word in ten. A thin woman with tally sticks at her belt has been watching you fail to buy honey.

A lane laid out by line between low reed roofs with goods set on their edges, the bay visible at its far end: a thin dark-browed woman with a linen headcloth and a bunch of tally sticks at her belt stands with one eyebrow raised before a pointing Frisian and a Wendish honey seller.
You understand nothing here, I can see it. I am Liuba. A piece of silver the size of your thumbnail, and you will understand everything.
The Frisian who says 'honey' as if it were a sneeze. You are better than last year. Not good. Better.
Listen. 'Med' is honey. 'Vosk' is wax. 'Ne' is no. With those three you can already be cheated properly.
The Dane at the awning told his man the king wants more than dues from this shore. He said it in Danish, in front of me, like a fool.
The stout Dane with the hazel switch buys the riders' Saxons. I do not turn words for him. I have seen his trade from the rope end.
Your countryman at the bead fire taught me Frisian. I taught him to count our way. He still says 'sixteen' as if it hurt.
Hire her tongue for this call (4 d)
Sit with her an evening and learn the market's words (8 d)
Offer her half
Point, hold up fingers, and manage without
Twenty blades

On the trampled grass above the town horses are picketed in lines. A broad man with a long moustache sits on a wagon tail where everyone can see him, one hand on the hilt of the only Frankish sword in the field.

Trampled grass with picketed horses: a broad Wend with dark hair cut round and a long moustache sits on a wagon tail, one hand on the hilt of a Frankish sword, the other open toward a Frisian skipper; behind him riders with round shields and spears, and no swords at all.
Frisian! You have a Frankish knife. Is there a bigger one in the boat? No? Look again, I will wait.
You are from the king's country. Then you are a guest twice. I ask a thing between the emperor's friends: twenty blades. No hilts needed. Paid in whatever your boat will hold.
I fought the king's Saxons for him on the Sventana field. His envoy stood beside me. My men fought with spears, and with what the Saxons dropped.
Your law says no blades to the Slavs. I am the Slav who guards your emperor's border. Explain it to me slowly.
We have Saxon fields now and nothing to turn them with. A rider with a plough. My mother would be pleased.
Open the casks on the grass: two swords for the prince
Offer two crates of ploughshares and tools instead
Say plainly that your king's law forbids it, and that you keep it
The spoil of the Sventana field
A wagon tail on the trampled grass is heaped with cloaks and brooches. Behind the wheel a row of roped Saxons sits in the shade, and a stout Dane with a hazel switch is pricing them by eye.

A wagon tail heaped with Saxon cloaks and brooches: a young long-armed Wendish rider in a quilted coat holds a woman's brooch up to the light; behind the wheel a row of bound Saxons sitting in the shade, one looking straight at the viewer; a stout Dane with a hazel switch walking the row.
On the Sventana field the Saxons ran into the river. We sold the cloaks dry. The owners were not consulted. Cloaks, knives, brooches. Look. All sound.
You are from the Frisian coast. I hear it. I do not ask to be bought. I ask which way the Danes' country lies, and how many days.
That one is a smith's son. The Dane has first pick and has not picked him yet. A hundred by weight and he is yours before the switch comes down the row.
Your Saxon mate has not come ashore. He is sitting in the boat with his back to the land.
Buy the smith's son, and carry him to the Danes' country (100 d)
Buy three Saxon cloaks off the wagon tail (30 d)
Tell him which way the Danes lie, and walk on
Three wells
Square mouths of split oak are let into the ground every few houses, each with a pole and a wooden bucket. A stocky man stands waist-deep in a fresh shaft, passing up buckets of grey clay.

A square well shaft lined with fresh yellow split oak: a stocky man in a round felt cap, clay to the thighs, passes up a bucket; women with yokes wait their turn; low reed roofs in straight rows behind.
Mind the hole. Water? That one by the lane is sweet. The one by the shore is for washing boats and Danes.
You are back. So is the water. Fill your casks at the new one. I want to hear what a stranger thinks of it.
A new shaft, the lining still yellow. People do not dig where they do not mean to stay. Drink. Say what you think. Take your time.
The old Dane who taught me to split oak is dead. He lies in a boat at the old ground. He was right about oak. I never told him.
They say the Danes at Ripa line their wells with old wine casks. A well in a barrel. I would be ashamed. Is it true?
You have whetstones from the north. I share one with four men. It is like sharing a wife.
Pay for the oak of his next well (40 d)
Give him whetstones of his own
Drink, and say the water is good
The wrights' end

At the north end of the shore two hulls stand on blocks: one riveted in the Danish way, one pegged with wooden nails. A bent old man with a tar-stained beard is looking at your boat as a leech looks at a wound.

The north end of a reedy shore: two hulls on blocks, one with iron rivets in neat lines and one with rows of wooden pegs; a steam trough smoking, oak chips ankle-deep; a bent old Dane with a white tar-stained beard and two fingers missing holds a rivet hammer.
That is a Frisian strake, and whoever fitted it was in a hurry. Pull her up. I will tell you what it costs to be ashamed of.
Still floating. I am a little surprised. Sit down. The trough is not hot yet.
The Wends peg their planks with wood and stuff the seams with moss. It holds. I have stopped telling them it should not.
My sister's son weighs for the king under that sail. I build for anyone. One of us sleeps well.
When I am done, see that they put me in the small boat, the one with the patched stem. Not the good one. Somebody can still use that.
A brother's son of mine mends boats at the river mouth in Skane. Tell him the old man still rivets. He will say I should peg. Tell him to come and say it.
The grey one in your boat and I pulled in one ship, once. He will not say where. Neither will I. It was wet.
Have him set the strake right (10 d)
Ask him for his marks into the bay
Promise to see him laid in the small boat
Let him get back to his hull
A boat for Toki
At the old ground a trench has been cut in the turf the length of a small boat. Danes and Wends stand round it with cups, a few paces apart, each after their own fashion.

A grave field of low mounds: a small clinker boat with a patched stem sunk to her gunwales in a trench, an old man laid in her with a rivet hammer on his chest and a dog at his feet; a mixed crowd of Danes and Wends standing round with cups; a lean Dane with a notched lip at the stem.
My mother's brother is dead. He built for anyone and belonged to nobody. His heirs want silver for the boat before it goes in the ground. I weigh for a king. Kings pay late.
He said a Frisian had promised to see it done properly. I did not believe him. He was right about most boats, too.
It should be the good boat. He said the patched one. He would. We are doing as he said, and complaining.
Pay toward the boat and the grave ale (40 d)
Take a spade and carry turf with the rest
Keep to the shore: he was not your dead
The amber pit
A pit hut with its door propped open for the light. Inside a narrow man in a short patched Frisian cloak turns an amber bead on a bow drill, squinting. He stops when he hears you speak to your crew.

A sunken hut seen from its doorway: a narrow squinting man in a patched short cloak, a small lead cross on a cord, works a bow drill on a half-drilled amber bead; a small crucible in the coals, strings of beads on a peg, burn scars on both hands.
That is terp mud on your boots or I never saw any. Say something. Anything. I have not heard it spoken right since the last ice.
The countryman. Come down into the pit, mind the crucible. Did you bring glass, or only yourself?
The bead-makers at Ripa get the Rhine glass first and send on what they do not want. If you see the old one there, tell him his leavings melt well enough.
They burn their dead here, or boat them, or bury them with a horse. I should like to say a Paternoster with a man who knows the words. Once a year would do.
I have a cousin at Dorestat on my mother's side, a widow with a storehouse. She thinks I am dead. She may be right.
In your chest are painted leaves from a gospel book. This man has not seen the words written since he was a boy.
Sell him a sack of raw glass for drilled amber
Give him a leaf of the gospel
Say the Paternoster with him at the bead fire
Three questions
A long-legged man in a grey riding cloak has come down from the farm above the strand, leading a saddled horse. He wears an old helmet with one gilded brow and a bare rivet where the other was.

A low shore of shingle and black weed at the head of a narrow bay: a long-legged Dane in a grey riding cloak with a worn ash spear and an old helmet with one gilded brow stands beside a saddled horse, facing a small Frisian boat; a farm on the rise behind.
Stand off a moment. Who are you, whose men, and what brings a keel that small this far up our water?
The Dorestat boat. You know the questions, so answer them and I will send the boy ahead.
No questions. Draw her up by mine. My wife has eels on, and the steward can wait an hour.
East wind tomorrow. The strand will be dry for a ship's length by noon. Lie afloat or lie a week.
Three long ships went out by the islands at first light, no cargo, shields inboard. More follow. As a friend: be somewhere else by midsummer, and not east.
Twelve keels went to the muster from this strand. I have counted seven home. The hall does not ask me. I do not say.
You are looking at the helmet. One brow. My father's father lost the other on this beach. I still look when the water is low.
Answer his three questions truly
Give a gift at the watch farm (6 d of silver, weighed)
Name the steward as the man who knows you
The steward's tally
By the hall's east door stands a sunken-floored house with the only lock in the place. Outside it a tall stooped man with an iron key the length of a hand waits beside a trestle and a folding scale.

A plank-roofed storehouse beside a great bowed hall: a tall stooped steward in a long brown tunic with a staff and a great iron key stands at a trestle with a folding scale and a whetstone for trying silver; casks and bundled hides in the dark doorway.
You came past the watch, so you are somebody's guest. Whose is still to be seen. What is in the boat?
The Frisian with the small boat. Your last cask was good. The one before it was not, and I have not forgotten either.
The hall drinks a cask in two nights when the following is home. I can count nights. So can you.
The women grind on stones their grandmothers wore hollow. A man with Rhine stone could name his weight here.
The king's household winters here now and eats what three halls would. I offer a split stick in place of silver: half now, half when the king's share comes home.
Your stick hangs with the others. The king's share is not yet home. When it is, you are paid before the skald.
The chief in the Vik sends his gift each year, and I weigh it in front of his man. He thinks it a slight. It is. It is also how I know what he can afford.
Sell him two casks of wine for weighed silver
Sell him two casks on the split stick: half now, half later
Take his order for Rhine querns
Say the boat holds nothing a hall wants
Dead men's tallies
Half the benches in the hall are dark. The steward has laid the split sticks out on the trestle by the store door at dusk, and yours is among them.
Dusk at a store door: a tall stooped steward holds half a split tally stick in each hand over a trestle covered with others; behind him the long hall with every second bench dark and unlit.
The king is dead, and the men who would have paid these are in the ground with two more kings. I set the boards for all of them anyway. It is not my place to count the dead.
What will you take for your half? Hides and bacon now, to the weight. Or leave it hanging, and I see it paid in silver if the hall lasts. Or nothing.
Put your stick on the long fire, with the bench watching
Take hides and bacon to the weight
Leave the stick hanging and wait
Tola's corner

A low house behind the hall with steam coming out under the eaves. On the bench outside, where the hall's people sit when they want to talk without the lord hearing, a broad woman with red forearms makes room.

A low thatched brew-house with steam under the eaves, bunches of bog myrtle drying, a great kettle on stones: a broad woman with red forearms, a linen head-cloth and a wooden ladle in her belt sits on a bench by the door holding out a cup.
A Frisian. Do they brew where you come from, or only sell other men's? Sit, tell me what honey costs in the south.
You again, and thinner. Does nobody feed you on that boat? Here. Drink it before the steward sees.
That grey one in your boat. He had fair hair and too many answers when I last saw him. Does he still?
The king is dead, cut down by a man of his own following. I had it before the hall did. I am brewing for a grave ale nobody has ordered yet.
Twelve went to the muster from this bench and I have brewed for seven since. Nobody has told the steward. He can count cups.
My honey comes from a farmer over the sound, by the river mouth in Skane. I pay him a year behind. He sends it all the same. That is what I call a neighbour.
There is a Tola at Ripa who sells ale by a well. Guests bring me her greetings. I send mine back. Neither of us has said anything new in ten years.
Sell her two crocks of honey for the brewing
Carry her silver over the sound to the farmer Hebbi
Fetch Ravn up from the boat to her bench
Drink what she pours and answer her questions
The hard ones

A house as long as six ships laid end to end, dark after the daylight. You are shown the low bench by the door. A slight man with a red-brown beard combed to a point comes down the hall to look at you.

The inside of a great hall seen from the low bench by the door: a long fire, benches along both walls, shields and hangings; a slight skald in a blue cloak a little too fine for him, ink-black fingers, a rune stick held up between two fingers.
A man from where the land is lower than the sea. Good. You will know what I mean by a house that swims.
The wave-horse rider is back. Have you an answer for me, or only silver? I take both.
The hard ones cost twelve pennyweights. The one I cannot answer myself is not for sale. Ask your grey steersman about it.
The hard ones are for men the hall knows. You it does not know yet. Come back when the steward has stopped asking whose guest you are.
That ribbon on your sleeve is from the river mouth in Skane. I paid her for one with a riddle about eight feet. She deserved a better. Carry her this one.
The steward will move me down the bench before the meat comes. He does it every feast. I make a verse about it every feast. We are both improving.
You have the look of a man with a hawk and a duck in his mouth. Say it across the fire, then, where the bench can hear.
Buy the hard one (12 d)
Answer him across the fire
Take his riddle to carry to the weaver
Sit on the low bench and listen
Swine and salt
A cart track beside a small clear stream, oak wood on one hand. Pigs root under the oaks, and a short thick man with a holly staff counts under his breath as you come up.

A stream valley with oak wood: pigs rooting under the trees, a short thick swineherd in an undyed hood with a holly staff and a horn on a cord, a lean yellow dog at his heel; on the rise ahead a great hall roof showing over the trees between round mounds.
Mind the sow. She has nine and trusts nobody. Are you for the hall? Then you want the steward, not me.
The boatman. I counted you last time. One of you, two feet. I got it right twice.
Here is one of my own, whatever the skald says. Ten tongues, twenty eyes, forty feet, and it moves along. You are looking at it.
Salt is short. If the killing comes at winter's start and the salt has not, half of this goes to the crows.
I have a cousin over the sound who herds by an old market and gives away verses on sticks. The same two verses. We had them from the same grandfather.
There is a path round the watch farm, by the alder carr. I did not tell you. The dogs know it too.
Sell him four sacks of salt for bacon
Take his riddle with you
Tell him what moves along on forty feet
Shut the hurdle behind you
Whoever sits in the chair
A small house set apart downwind of the hall, with moulds of baked clay broken by the door. Inside a man bent at the neck holds something on the end of a pin at arm's length, and frowns at it.

A small smithy with a knee-high clay hearth and a stump for an anvil: a burn-pocked hand holds a silver figure no bigger than a fingertip up to the light of the door, someone seated on a chair with two birds on its arms; fine tongs, a singed beard tied in a knot.
Do not stand in the light. What have you got? If it is quicksilver, shut the door and name your weight.
The southerner. Your silver rang true last time. Put it there. Not on the moulds.
Look. On the pin. The height of your thumbnail. Somebody in a chair, two birds on the arms. I need quicksilver to gild it, and I have none.
It is done. Half the hall says the High One with his ravens. My wife says it is wearing her apron. Whoever sits in the chair, that is who it is.
My scale is older than I am. It came from a caster at Ripa, they say, of my mother's kin. It folds. It has never been wrong, which is more than I can say for the kin.
The town smiths at the Slie cast by the hundred from one model. It shows. They buy all the quicksilver that comes north, so that nobody else can show them up.
Sell him a flask of quicksilver, and ask no questions
Take his order for quicksilver
Ask him who the figure is
Four cups and a weight
The hall's benches are scrubbed and empty. At the store door a heavy old man with a white moustache has set four silver cups on the trestle, and a lead weight cased in bronze beside them.

An empty great hall, benches scrubbed bare: at a trestle a heavy old steward with a white moustache and a thin good cloak stands over four silver cups, one worked with beasts, and a bronze-cased weight; a single lamp; through the door, far off over water, a small church.
You want Roskilde. Everyone does. It is an hour's row east. Or you could sit, and I could find a cup.
Four cups and a weight. The hall's last table silver. One is foreign work, with beasts. What do such things fetch in the south? Must they be melted to fetch it?
The priest across the water has the king's word that the old hall's goods are the king's. He would rather have them given than taken. I set the dogs on him. Politely.
The king has a bell over there now. On a still morning I hear it. On a still morning I shut the door.
I have a clay pot and I have chosen a place. A man would need somebody to hold the lamp. He would not need him to remember where.
Hold the lamp for him, and do not ask to be told the place
Talk him into giving the cups to the church across the water
Buy the four cups by weight, for the pot at the Slie (280 d)
The seat at Salhaugar

Two low mounds by a farm, and against the nearer one a seat of flat stones facing the yard. An old man sits there with a horn in his lap and a boy to lead him. His eyes are white. He turns his head before you have spoken.

Two low grass mounds beside a farm in barley fields: on a seat of flat stones a thin old man with white hair to his shoulders and clouded eyes, an old blue cloak, a bronze-rimmed drinking horn in his lap, a boy's hand on his arm; three interlocked horns cut on the door post behind.
A step I do not know, and a second I have not heard for a long time. Sit. Which of you speaks first?
The merchant. You walk more surely than you did. Have you answers, or more questions? Either will do.
My son cut the sticks and I set them. He is in the new mound. The sticks are still on the road.
A ferryman, a shipman of the Vik, a singer among the Svear, a carter at Ripa. They sat on one low bench by a door. They hand on what I set. Did you think riddles grew on ships?
There is one I set that is not to be answered. Your grey seaman answered it, when he had fair hair. Bring him up the path. I should like to hear him not answer it.
I give you a thing for your chest, for the walk you took. It is what a guest should know at any door, this one too.
Take the old man's verse for your chest
Stand back, and let Ravn stand before the seat
Tell him a thing he does not know
Across the water
An hour's row east of the old strand, on a slope above a spring-fed cove, stands a wooden church with a shingled roof and a bell. It smells of new-cut oak. A priest is sweeping the step.

A wooden church with a shingled roof and a small bell on a slope above a cove, a king's house beside it and booths going up along the shore: a spare priest in a plain dark habit with a birch broom on the step; a small Frisian boat nosed into the cove.
You came up the old fjord and landed at the old strand, so you walked past a dead hall to find a living church. Most do it the other way now.
The merchant. Good. Sit. I hear confessions in three tongues and bad Danish, and yours I can follow.
The steward at the old hall has four silver cups and no lord to drink from them. I asked for them for the altar. He set his dogs on me. Politely, I grant him.
Three of the old hall's cups are a chalice and a dish now. The fourth, with the beasts, I kept as it was. I could not say why. It looked at me.
The king has given us a bishop, hallowed over the sea among the English. Bremen is not pleased. I am from Saxony, and I say nothing, in three tongues.
At Christmas a great man was killed in this church at the king's word, after a quarrel over a board game. I scrubbed the floor myself.
A pilot at the river mouth in Skane sends me herring every Lent. I signed him with the cross when he was a boy. He keeps a hammer under his shirt for the bar. I have not asked to see it.
Hear Mass under the shingle roof
Give alms at the door (8 d)
Sell him two cakes of wax for the altar
The halved penny

Three plots downwind where the hearths are. A thick-armed man with a beard singed on one side is weighing scrap bronze against a row of lead weights. He holds out his hand for your silver without looking up.

A caster's blackened hands over a small bronze folding scale on a chest lid: in one pan lead weights, in the other half a silver penny, the other half lying beside a chisel; a Frisian in a short cloak staring at it; crucibles glowing in charcoal behind.
Put it in the pan. Your king's face I do not know. His silver I will know in a moment.
The Frisian with the whole pennies. They weighed true last time. I said so on the bank. Put them in the pan.
He nicks one penny to see the colour inside, sets another on a block, and cuts it across the king's name with a chisel. He hands you half. He does not see why you are staring.
A stamp is one man's word. A scale is the same for everyone.
A man paid me with silver from the east last moon, with writing like worm tracks. Purest I have melted. I kept one piece uncut.
A Dane sets up his scale among the Ests each summer with weights off the same mould as mine. If he and I agree, and you do not, it is not the weights.
You have a scale now. Whose? Show me the weights. Hm. Honest. I would have made the pan deeper.
Buy a folding scale and his own weights (36 d)
Keep the two halves to show at home
Insist on paying by count, whatever the count is called (3 d over)
Watch him weigh, and say nothing
The thing with eight feet

A sunken hut with the door-flap tied back and four women in the light of it. One, small and straight, weaves a patterned ribbon on a little antler comb held in her lap, and looks you over without stopping her hands.

A sunken hut seen from its doorway: a small woman with a spindle turning from her left hand and a ribbon on an antler comb in her lap looks up with one eyebrow raised; three other women at spindles behind her; in the corner of the door frame, a spider in its web against the light.
You are looking at the ribbon. Everyone does. Look with your eyes. Now: what has eight feet and four eyes, and carries its knees above its belly?
The Frisian who thinks before he answers. Sit. Eight feet, four eyes, knees above the belly. I have not changed it.
You have it. I see it. Say it, then, and the women will stop pretending to spin.
Your cloak hangs by my fire. Sleep there. The boat is damp, and I want the news before Asbod has it.
A man of the king's hall on the isles paid for a ribbon with that riddle. He has harder ones he sells dear. A woman who pays in thread deserves better, I told him.
You have something from the skald. I can tell by how carefully you are not saying it.
Bring me red dye. Madder. This country grows sheep and opinions.
Take her riddle away with you
Say what has eight feet
Say the skald's riddle to her
Watch the ribbon grow, and say nothing
Asbod's bench

A house on the ground like the others, with the door open and a bench outside it. Inside, a long hearth, a vat, and men of four peoples sitting where they can see the door. Somebody is moving amber pieces across squares scratched on a stone.

A long hearth and an ale vat under a smoky roof: a broad red-armed woman with a dipper at her belt and two brooches that do not match; men of several peoples on the benches watching the door; by the fire a flat stone scratched with squares and three amber gaming pieces.
A new face, and a boat with a tent on her. There is fire, water and a bench. Ale is silver, by Alle's weight. Sit by the door till I know you.
You. Further in this time. The man in your old seat is from Gotland and says he is from nowhere. What did you bring me to tell?
A great man inland sent to say the bank owes him a share. We sent back a comb. Nobody has come to argue.
Ships from the west talk of a church burnt on an island and silver going cheap. I have not seen any of it here. Yet.
You are a man short. I can see it in how the boat lies. There is one on my bench looking for a ship. He left the last one over a share, not a knife. I asked.
The grey Northman sat on that bench the season before he went south. I kept his place a year. Tell him it is gone now. Tell him gently.
The wright has drunk at my fire every evening for three years and said nothing useful. If you have a word for him, say it. Somebody must.
Take the hand she names (4 d to bind him)
Pay for the bench's ale, and listen (3 d)
Sit by the door and say where you are from
Antler in spring
A fenced plot on the oldest strip, right above the bank. In a hut sunk knee-deep in the sand a lean man saws antler into plates by the light of the door, and does not look up.

A sunken hut with its roof at shoulder height on a fenced sandy plot: a lean man in a leather apron white with antler dust saws comb plates at a bench by the door, a finished comb pushed through his belt; a dog gnawing under the bench; the river below.
A Frisian. Your cloak gives you away. Sit where the dust does not blow. Combs are in the chest, brooches on the peg. Touch what you like.
I know that hand. You took two dozen and paid fair weight. Did they sell, or have you come to complain?
My father made beads across the river. Then ships brought beads by the sack. He learned combs at forty. I keep that in mind.
Tofi at the Slie sends his greeting? He sends his prices, wrapped in a greeting. Tell him the same from me, in the same wrapping.
Lay down a stake on my plot at the winter nights, and I work it till the ships go out. Combs and brooches with your mark on, worth twice the stake. Then I need not sail the coast so far.
Your stake is in the chest with your mark on the lid. It is not combs yet. Antler does not hurry and neither do I.
Sell him two bundles of shed antler for combs
Lay down a stake in his workshop for the winter (60 d)
Buy two dozen combs at the maker's price (18 d)
Turn the combs over, and put them back
Your mark on the back plate
On Toke's plot a chest stands open on the bench, with a mark cut on its lid that you know. It is half full of combs in rows and brooches in pairs. Thjodvi has the key.

A sunken workshop by lamplight: a small straight woman with a spindle in one hand and a key in the other stands beside an open chest with a merchant's mark cut on its lid, rows of finished combs and paired bronze brooches inside; antler dust on everything.
Toke cut your mark on the back plate of every one. Nobody asked him to. He said: sell them as yours.
Six dozen combs and two pairs of brooches. Count them. He counted twice and I a third time, which is the one to trust.
Take your share of the winter's work
Take it, and leave the same stake for next winter (60 d)
Hebbi's stick

On the bare trodden square a heavy-shouldered farmer has laid a sack of antler and a sack of amber on a hide. A short stick cut with runes is stuck in his belt. He looks at your scale as a man looks at a strange dog.

A bare trodden square among fenced plots: a weathered heavy-shouldered farmer in a brown tunic and leg wrappings stands over a hide with shed antler and a sack of raw amber, a short rune-cut stick in his belt; women stringing beads behind.
You buy? Antler, shed this spring. Amber from the shore, a sackful. I want iron or a fair weight. I will know if it is not fair. Somehow.
The stranger who paid what he said. That is rare enough to remember. I kept the best tines back.
My cattle graze where the old market was. They come home with glass in their hooves. Blue, mostly.
You have come from the king's isle. The brew-wife there owes me for a year of honey. She always pays. A year behind, like the seasons.
Here. A stick. My father's verse about the herd that knows when to go home, and the fool who does not. Keep it dry.
I have a cousin who herds swine for the king's hall. He gives away the same verses and says he made them.
Trade him a crate of iron tools for amber and antler
Hand over Tola's silver, to the grain
Take the stick
Tell him the weight is fair, and wait while he decides whether to believe it
The rivet bank

The upstream end of the bank. A boat lies on her side on rollers with three strakes off, and a tall big-handed man drives old rivets out of them into a basket. Beyond him a fire of grey boat planks burns with a green edge.

A sandy river bank: a clinker boat on her side on rollers with three strakes off, a tall sandy-haired wright with tar to the elbows knocking rivets into a basket; behind him a fire of old boat planks burning green at the edges; split oak stacked beside.
She is Danish-built, or close to it. Four oars. Somebody has looked after her. Draw her up here and I will look at her garboards.
Your boat again. She floats higher than she did. You have been selling. Has the fourth strake wept since I caulked it?
With the wind in the east the bar breaks white. Wait a tide. I have pulled three men out who would not wait.
This country grows no straight oak. I burn old boats for their rivets and mend with what the fire leaves. Bring oak and I take a third off any work.
My father's brother builds among the Wends at Reric. He rivets. They peg. He says a pegged hull is patience. I say it is a pegged hull.
My father's brother died among the Wends. They laid him in his own boat, I hear. The patched one. He would.
I drink at Asbod's every evening. It is good ale. That is all I have to say about it.
Have him caulk and tar her (8 d)
Take his order for oak
Tell Asbod, in his hearing, that the wright mends well and talks badly
Wait a tide on his word about the bar
A Wend on the bank
A broad boat pegged with wood lies among the Danish ones, looking foreign. A man in a fur-edged cap sits on her gunwale eating smoked fish. He stops chewing when he sees what you are holding.

A broad shallow boat with rows of wooden pegs along her planks drawn up among slimmer Danish boats on a river bank: a Wend in a fur-edged cap on her gunwale, a piece of smoked fish in one hand, the other held out for a notched tally stick.
This is Dragomir's cutting. I know the notch. Dragomir of Reric? They said the Danes had him. They say many things.
His wife's brother holds the fort by the long lake. I pass under it in nine days. I carry this for nothing. A house that fed me twice is owed a thing carried.
Give him the tally, and tell him where Dragomir sits now
Give him the tally, and buy a cake of his wax (36 d)
The herring shore
North of the river mouth small boats run up on the sand before noon, silver to the gunwales, and the gulls stand over them like smoke. Women gut on boards. The tubs want more salt than anyone has.

An autumn beach north of a river mouth: small boats heaped with silver herring run up on the sand, gulls thick overhead, women gutting on boards beside wooden tubs; a fisherman with a wicker scoop looks hopefully at a small trading boat.
Herring. Take them or the gulls will. Salted, they keep to the Rhine. Unsalted, they keep till evening. You see my trouble.
That is salt in your boat. Bay salt, grey. Do not name a weight. Name a number of barrels.
The man in the stone house takes a share of what is landed now. He did not catch them. He does not gut them. He has a ladder.
You promised salt for this autumn. The women have been asking about you by name. It is not always a good sign.
Trade four sacks of salt for two barrels of herring
Buy two barrels, salted, by weight of silver (16 d)
Promise salt for next autumn
Stand upwind and watch
The chest lid

The river meets the bay over sand. Upriver, where a town was, there is barley. A spare woman with a small antler comb at her belt sells from the lid of a chest, and a boy watches your boat as if he means to remember her.

A river mouth over sand with surf on the bar: a spare woman in a blue strap dress with two old oval brooches worn smooth and a slotted antler comb at her belt sits behind a chest whose lid is laid with combs and folded cloth; barley fields upriver where a town was.
You are looking for a town. It was up there, where the barley is. I was born on the fourth plot from the bank. What do you want to buy?
The Frisian house. Your people bought combs of mine. Of my people's. Sit. The chest lid is the market now.
The plough turned up a mould for a brooch last spring. My uncle's. I knew the pattern. The farmer gave it to his child to play with.
I keep one stick of a longer question, the fourth of five. My brother the pilot was given it against a fare. It goes to whoever brings the answer to the one before, and to nobody else.
A woman of my kin asked your forefather a riddle, and he answered. So I ask you one, and it is harder, and worth more.
An Englishman sailed past for the Ests' country and put in for water. He asked who we pay. I said: whoever comes.
Give the answer to the stick before hers, and take the fourth
Buy cloth and combs off the chest lid (20 d)
Ask where the town's families went
Both kings won
There are more ships in the bay than you have seen in your life, gilded prows from edge to edge, and they are not all one king's. A boy of sixteen has waded out to take your bow line.

A river mouth seen from the dunes of the sand bar: the bay beyond packed with striped sails and gilded prows from edge to edge, smoke rising behind; in front, one small trading boat being pulled toward the reeds by a boy holding her bow line.
You had better choose a side of the river and stay on it. South is King Cnut, with English and Danes. North are the Svear and the Northmen. Both sides want food.
The king's stewards pay in English pennies, by count, and want more than you have. Bread, grain, salt meat, rope. Name it and it is sold.
Or pull her into the reeds up the river, where I am going. From there a man sees a great deal of water, and nobody asks him anything.
Sell four sacks of rye to Cnut's stewards on the south side
Sell four sacks of rye to the north side, by weight
Draw the boat into the reeds upriver and wait it out
The pilot at the bar
A wiry man in a faded red wool cap stands in the shallows off the bar with a sounding pole in his hand, as if he had been waiting for you since the last full moon.

Surf on a sand bar at a river mouth: a wiry man in a faded red wool cap and a short sea cloak stands thigh-deep with a sounding pole, a small silver cross on a thong at his neck; behind him the river, an alder, and later a grey stone house with its door above a ladder.
You will want taking in. The sand moved at the last full moon. A fee now, or a bigger one to the wright's grandson when you are aground.
I know your boat. She draws a hand more than you say she does. Follow my pole. Did I tell you about the fleets?
Some say the Northmen dammed the river and loosed it on the king's ships. I was here. I saw no dam. I saw a great deal of water.
Your house had a boat in the reeds that summer, beside me. So you know what I saw. Do not tell the bench. The dam is the one they pay for.
The stone house has a door you reach by ladder. A man who wants to keep you out that badly means to take something from you.
There is a priest in the stone house now, the bishop's man. He asked if I was baptised. I said signed. He said that is a door, not a house. I said I pilot. I know about doors.
Pay his fee and follow his pole (4 d)
Ask him what he really saw that summer
Take her in yourself, on the alder and the green water
The chief's gift

High over the bay the long roof of the hall catches the sun. A tall spare man in a red cloak has come down the road between the barrows with two grey hounds, and stands looking at your boat as at a horse he might buy.

A sheltered bay with boats on rollers and a long hall roof on the height above: a tall spare chief with grey in a fair beard, a red cloak pinned with a silver ring pin, a gold-bound horn in his hand and two grey hounds at his knee, stands on the shingle before a small Frisian boat.
A Frisian, in a boat that size. Sit. A man who comes so far in so little has sense or has none, and I like to know which.
You came back, and the boat is no bigger. Good. Men who grow fast leave fast.
I take no toll. I take a gift, and then you are my guest, and who robs my guest has robbed me. It comes cheaper than a toll.
Posts are being driven on my shore and plots pegged out. People say the king of the Danes wished it. I say I did. A plot may be had by anyone I call guest.
A ship's chief from the west sells on my strand and gives small gifts. Gilt things with holes in them. The women buy and the men laugh.
Two kings of the Danes are coming to ask whether I am theirs. Two kings, for one answer. It is a great honour and I could do without it.
Give the guest's gift (8 d of silver, weighed)
Give a cask of wine to the hall
Greet him as his guest of last year
