Give him news in place of a gift, and trade from the boat
Thordis's bench
A low house with a long hearth and a soapstone pot the size of a shield over the fire. A broad woman fills horn cups from a tub without looking at them, and looks at everybody else.

A low earth-floored house with a hearth down the middle and a great soapstone pot on chains: a broad woman with strong forearms and a ladle in her belt like a weapon fills horn cups from a tub; through the gable door, the bay and boats.
You are the Frisian with the small boat. Bard said one would come. A jug is a sliver of silver, and the first is not counted.
Your place is the end of the bench by the door. I kept a drunk Dane out of it this morning. You may thank me.
A Dane bought three English boys on this strand, the autumn after the raid west. A fourth the crew kept: he counted my cups without being asked. He was right, too.
The counting boy came through again three summers on, in the Dane's boat, bound east. He knew my cups. He did not know me. I gave him bread, and he held it like a thing to be tallied.
The gilt things on the dealer's cloth came off a god's house over the sea. The women wear them. I would not. Somebody is missing them.
The chief's wife on the Karmsund sends me down for my bed, and I send her bead strings. We have never met. I know her by what she will not buy.
Bard's son is back from the west with a silver cup and nothing to say. He will not ship with that chief again. He might with a man who only sells things.
Ask who the Dane was, and where the crew took the fourth
Take Bard's son as a hand (4 d to bind him)
Pay your tally and stand her a cup (3 d)
Drink the first jug, the one that is not counted
The drowned chief
A Dane you do not know has moved along the bench until he is beside you. He lowers his voice in the way of a man who wants the whole house to hear.

The ale bench by firelight: a lean Dane leans close to a Frisian merchant, one hand already round the merchant's jug, mouth open in mid-story; behind them a broad ale-wife with a ladle, looking at the ceiling.
You have not heard? Thorleif of the Karmsund is drowned, ship and all, off the Stad. His widow is selling the swords and the tusks for what she can get. I had it from a man who saw the wreck.
A quick boat that got there before the Danes did would fill her hold for a third of the price. I would go myself, but my skipper is a cautious man. Is that jug yours?
He sat there last summer too. He had a drowned chief then as well. A different one.
Stand him the jug and hear the rest (2 d)
Thank him, and carry the news south as it stands
Ask Thordis what she thinks of him
A man's grip

An open-sided shed set back from the houses for fear of fire. A very wide man with burn scars up both forearms holds a sword blade to the light by its bare tang. On the wall hang hilts without blades.

A forge shed at night: a wide scarred smith bends a bright blade across his knee, a Frisian watching with his hand half raised to stop him; a boy at a bellows of two goatskins; a row of hilts without blades, bronze and walrus tooth, on the wall behind.
Show me your knife. No, the edge, not the handle. Hm. Frisian iron. It will cut cheese.
You again. Have you brought iron, or only talk? I can have talk from my wife.
Bring me blades bare. The Frankish hilt is a clerk's hilt. I put a man's grip on it, and we share what it fetches.
The Franks' king forbids his blades to leave his land. So they cost more, and come anyway, under salt. I do not ask under what.
Thorleif of the west coast wants six swords hilted before the cuckoo. He pays in walrus tooth. Good for grips, bad for bread.
You are standing like a man with something under his ballast. Bring it. I bend it to my knee. If it comes back straight, I buy.
I learned casting from a goldsmith at the Danes' summer market. He weighed me before he taught me. Like everybody else.
Sell him two bare blades to hilt
Take his standing order for bare blades
Buy a keg of his rivets at the forge's price (12 d)
Tell him no, and tell him why
The first of three sisters

A lean stooped man sits on an upturned boat above the tide line with a sounding line coiled over his shoulder and a rune-cut stick in his belt. He has been watching you come in, and did not think much of it.

A curve of grey shingle under bare rock: a lean stooped skipper with a white scar through one eyebrow and a sealskin hood pushed back sits on an upturned boat holding up a rune-cut stick; lines of white-topped waves run in past skerries behind him.
You came in between the wrong two skerries and lived. Either you are lucky or Ravn is aboard. Ah. Ravn is aboard.
You came in between the wrong two skerries and lived. That is luck. Do not lean on it.
The small boat. I knew the sail before the hull. Next time keep the bare rock to steerboard until the hall roof opens.
I had one off a bench, long ago. Who are the maids that go weeping to the joy of their father? White hoods, fair hair, wide awake in a gale. Take your time. They do.
There are two more. A ferryman on the Slie has the third and gives it for the fare. A singer among the Svear has the second and sells it, as singers do.
You have her. Then walk out along the rocks with me at low water. I show you the way in. Once. I do not repeat myself.
There is an old steersman on the Karmsund who says no man of the Vik can find his sound without following a better ship. I have found it twenty times. I follow the land. It is always there.
Take the stick with the riddle cut on it
Answer him, and walk the rocks at low water
Ask Ravn for the answer, where Bard can hear
Ask him the days to the Heaths, and where to lie each night
A sale at night
A man from the high valleys is standing beside your boat with his hand on a bundle of your whetstones. Behind him a long thin man with a hazel rod has come to hear what is said.

A wide heath of ling and juniper with a ring of low stones and one standing stone: a long thin lawman with a hazel rod and a bag of lead weights round his neck stands between a Frisian merchant and an angry valley farmer holding a bundle of grey whetstones; men sitting on the ground in their cloaks.
Those hones in your boat are mine. My brother sold them off the sledge at night, while I was drunk at the bench. He had no right, and you had no witnesses.
Hear it once. A sale is good with two witnesses and a handshake. A sale at night is no sale. If you bought at night, you found it.
The thing sits when the sun is over the standing stone. Bring two who saw the bargain, or your silver, or the hones. Knives stay in belts on the heath.
You bought by daylight, by weight, on your own scale, and half the lane watched you do it.
Go up to the heath with two witnesses from the lane
Pay the man for his half of the sledge (10 d)
Hand back two bundles and keep the peace
The lake before a crossing

A long still lake among alders, dark as a whetstone and without a boat on it. On a flat rock at the water's edge lie a bead, a bent knife and a clipping of silver. An old woman with an iron staff sits a little way off and watches who comes.

A long still dark lake among alders: a flat rock at the water's edge with a bead, a bent knife and a bowl of butter on it; a small straight old woman with a white plait and a dark blue cloak sits apart with an iron staff across her knees.
A Christian. I can smell the wax. Stand where you are. The lake does not mind you, and neither do I, at that distance.
You again, and still alive. Then what I told you was true, or you did not listen. Either way you owe me.
The grey Northman has gone to the water first, put something small on the flat rock, and only then nodded to the old woman. She marks it.
It is the first day of summer by our count. The ships go into the water and the lake gets its share. Butter, a bead, a clipping of silver. Not blood, whatever your priests say.
You want to know if the crossing is good. Look at the gulls, then at your ropes. If both are sound, pay me anyway. I have told you true.
There is another with a staff on the Karmsund. She reads the swell and calls it seeing. I call it guessing. Tell her so if you pass.
You have been to the Karmsund, and you are carrying something of hers. Say it. I have been called worse by better.
Flat water. Hm. A thing seen in flat water stays where it was put. Tell her that, if you pass again. She will not like it. Good.
Pay her, and ask about the crossing (3 d)
Lay a clipping of silver on the flat rock, as Ravn did (1 d)
Tell her what the woman on the Karmsund said: anyone can see in flat water
Stand where you are, and wish her good day
Curios on a cloth
Between the hones and the soapstone a dealer has church things laid out on a cloth as curios: a little box shaped like a house, a cup, and painted calfskins the women buy for the knotwork.

A cloth on trodden earth between bundles of grey hones and soapstone bowls: a small house-shaped box with a ridged lid, a silver cup, and painted calfskin leaves with knotted beasts; a dealer squatting behind it, women bending to look.
From over the sea, last summer. The box had bones in it. I tipped them out. Nobody buys bones. The cup is silver. Weigh it yourself.
The skins are for patterns. A weaver took two. I do not know what the marks say. If you know, do not tell me. I would have to raise the price.
A west-coast chief with a red beard sold me the lot, and three English boys to a Dane beside me. A fourth he kept, who could count. I remember that one. He counted my hones.
You have been taught what such a leaf is worth where it was made. Here it is a pattern for a ribbon.
Buy the box and the cup by weight (40 d)
Buy the painted skins as patterns (6 d)
Ask where the chief with the red beard winters
The Frisian's house

One plot is kept differently: the fence mended, a bench outside the door, Rhineland jugs on a shelf. A short man in a cloak too short for the weather is counting cloth bolts against a tally stick, and stops at the sound of your voice.

A fenced plot with a small house whose gable door faces the bay: a short man with a long moustache and a striped cloak too short for the north counts cloth bolts against a tally stick; Rhineland jugs on a shelf, a dark lava quern by the hearth, a small wooden cross inside the door.
God keep you. Frisian? From where? Speak slowly, I want every word. Nobody here can say 'butter' properly.
Come in, mind the hearth. I have Rhine wine in a jug with tin on it, and nobody to drink it with who knows what it is.
Dorestat burned, so I left. Here I live among the men who do it, and they pay on the day. Nobody robs his own market.
No priest north of the Danes' wall. On Sundays I say what I remember and my wife corrects me. If you know the Creed whole, stay to supper.
There is a Frisian priest at Ripa now, they tell me, saying Mass on a sea chest. That is the nearest Mass to my door. Five days and a wall.
Men of this fjord were on the Loire. There was an altar cup in the market. I bought it. It has lain in the meal chest, under the meal, ever since. Now there is a priest to take it to.
Leave your wine with me over winter. I charge a twentieth and I do not drink it. I say so because my neighbours offer cheaper.
Take the altar cup to carry to the priest at Ripa
Sell him two casks of Rhine wine
Say the Creed with him at supper
Grass in the lanes

Grass grows in the lanes between the plots, and the inner jetty stands in mud at every state of the water. A long thin white-haired man with a hazel rod is waiting by the stone, with a bag of lead weights round his neck.

A shore of sunken house floors and leaning fence posts under a wide pale sky, grass in the lanes, one rotten jetty: a long thin white-haired man with a hazel rod stands beside a single small boat and a stack of bundled hones; a household loading a loom into another boat.
A stranger with goods. Then hear it once: weights are tried at the stone, quarrels wait for the thing, and knives stay in belts on the heath.
You know the law here by now. There is less of it than there was, and fewer to break it.
The bay is shallower than when I was a boy. I wade as a man where my father moored. The young say I have grown. I have not.
The hone men have come down with a sledge load and no other buyer. Do Frisians still want hones? How many can a boat like yours carry?
We are going to the Irish shore, where my man's brother has a plot by the black pool. Loom, quern, hearth stones. We have more than our boat will hold.
You may be the last keel I see here. I will witness your bargain all the same. Somebody should remember it was done properly.
Buy the whole sledge of hones, witnessed (40 d)
Take the household's loom and quern aboard as far as your next port, for a fare
Stand witness to another man's bargain at the stone
Who commands
A grey shingle beach in a narrow sound, ship-tents pitched ashore. In the morning a bent old man in a sealskin cap comes down the path from the hall, leaning on a staff cut from an old oar.

A grey shingle beach in a narrow sound, ships drawn up bow first with striped ship-tents beside them: a bent old man with a white beard to his chest, a sealskin cap and a staff cut from an oar comes down a path from a turf-roofed hall and a tall leaning stone.
Who commands here, and what is the errand? Speak up, boy. The gulls are louder than you.
You again. The boat is still afloat, then. I told them it would be. I did not believe it.
A gift for the hall goes up the path in plain sight, in your own hands. Not sent. Not hidden in a cloak. That is how it should be, so that is how it is.
Swell from the north-west and no wind in it. By evening there will be wind in it. Stay on the strand tonight.
They are laying the old lord in his boat on the ridge. I held the horse at the last one. I am too stiff to hold this one. They have given the halter to a boy.
Keep the tall stone over the boat-house roof until the black skerry opens. Then steer for the notch. Say it back to me.
Here is one for a long watch. Whence did winter come, and the warm summer, first of all? I had it from a man who had it from the wind.
Carry a gift up the path in plain sight (6 d of silver, weighed)
Say his marks for the sound back to him without a mistake
Take his question for the watch
Answer him: a Frisian, with goods, for the hall
A blade for a tusk

One long room under a turf roof, a fire down the middle. In the high seat a big wind-burned man with a red-fair beard holds a pair of walrus tusks across his knees, and looks at the plain sword on your belt.

Firelight in a long hall: a big red-bearded man in a blue tunic with tablet-woven braid and a silver neck ring holds a pair of walrus tusks across his knees, looking at the sword on a Frisian merchant's belt; the benches behind him leaning in to hear.
A Frisian in a boat that size, this far north. Either you are brave or your steersman is lost. Sit down either way.
The small boat again. My men have a wager on how long she floats. I have my silver on you.
You look at me as a man looks at a debt he thought was buried. Who said I drowned? I was wet. It is not the same thing.
Your king forbids you to sell me a sword. I do not see your king. I see you, and a boat with a ballast of stones. A pair of tusks for a sword. I say it aloud so the benches hear.
That is Asulf's cutting. He sends a Frisian to tell me what I owe. He could have sent a Dane. He means me to feel it.
We made a good landing in the west. The men there keep their silver on a table and their door open. Strange people.
Your grey man and I know each other of old. Ask him how. He will tell you about the weather.
Sell him a sword for tusks
Offer malt for the store instead, and say why
Give him Asulf's stick
Say you carry no swords, and hear his price
The swineherds

Above the farm the land rises to bare heather, and along the skyline stands a row of low mounds older than anyone's reckoning. Swine root between them. The boy who watches them has cropped hair growing out and a stick notched down its length.

A bare heath with a row of low mounds on the skyline: two thin boys in sack tunics with sticks among rooting swine, one writing in the mud, the other with a notched stick looking straight out at the viewer; the open sea grey to the west, a sound bright to the east.
You are not one of them. Speak low. Are you from the Franks? Do you know the island of Saint Cuthbert?
The Frisian. I cut a notch the day you left. I count the Sundays, so that somebody does.
The other one is Tidwine. He cries at night and writes letters in the mud with his stick. They will sell him first. He can do a thing they want.
Tidwine went east in the Dane's boat, the summer after the new mound. I have a notch for the day. He did not look back. I told him not to.
Tell the bishop Cuthred is alive and keeps the days. Have my name read at the altar, so that I am not counted dead. That costs you nothing.
The chief sells for silver by weight or for a sword. Half a mark a boy. Never for prayers. He said so, and laughed first.
Promise to carry his name to the bishop
Say a psalm with him, low, among the swine
Go down to the hall and ask the chief's price
Half a mark a boy

In the hall the chief has heard why you were on the heath. He laughs first. Beside the high seat his wife stands with her keys and a folding scale, and on her breast, among the oval brooches, a square gilt one that was the corner of a book.

A long hall by firelight: a big red-bearded chief laughing in the high seat; beside him a straight-backed woman with keys, a folding scale and a square gilt brooch on her breast; near the door a thin boy with a notched stick, watching a Frisian merchant's hands.
The English boys? They eat, they herd, they pray to the swine. Half a mark of silver each. Prayers I have enough of.
Or one good sword for the pair. A man who wants them home should not wait. A Dane comes by who buys what can count.
There is one now. The other could tally, and went east. For the one that is left: half a mark, or the sword.
My husband sells cheap when he has had ale. I do not. But a boy who keeps the Sundays on a stick eats more than he herds. Take him, if you have the weight.
Pay a mark of weighed silver for both boys (130 d)
Give a sword for the boys
Pay half a mark for Cuthred alone (65 d)
Say you have not the weight today
The woman with the keys

A squat log house on stone footings beside the hall, its door bound with iron and a woman's key in the lock. Inside, in the half dark: soapstone pots nested in hay, bundles of grey whetstones, sacks of down. She has the scale in her hand already.

A dim log storehouse: a straight-backed woman with fair hair under a linen cloth, keys and a folding scale at her belt and a square gilt brooch on her breast, stands among soapstone pots nested in hay, bundled whetstones and sacks of down; light from the iron-bound door.
You have come to trade. You will trade with me. My husband gives things away when he has had ale. What is in the boat?
The Frisian. Your last malt was honest weight. Do not look pleased. I weighed it twice to be sure.
The men came home with silver and two boys. I asked for corn. Nobody takes a corn bin in a raid.
On her breast, beside the two oval brooches, is a third: square, gilt, with rivet holes at the corners. It was the corner of a book.
You are looking at my angelica bed. Then here: who are the women of the mountain, where a maid bears a son by a maid, and none has a husband? They grow behind my hall.
The ale-wife in the Vik sends me bead strings by any ship coming west. I pay her in down. We have never met. I know her by her knots.
Nothing from over the sea leaves this store until you have seen it. I said so, and I do not say things twice.
Sell her four sacks of malt for goods from the store
Ask her about the square brooch
Take her riddle of the angelica bed
Let her weigh your silver, and say nothing
Glass for the mound

The old lord of the ness sits propped in the high seat and does not speak. Nobody on the farm will be surprised by a second mound on the ridge. The woman with the keys has something to ask of a man who trades in the south.

A boat sunk in a trench on a windy ridge, half covered with turf: a woman in a strap dress sets a thin glass beaker among wooden bowls and bedding at a dead man's side; a thin dark poet in a red cloak stands by with a rune stick; the sound grey below.
The old one will not see another winter. He must lie in a boat, with good things. I want glass for him. A tall clear cup, the best you can find, by the time the corn is cut next year.
On the ridge north of the farm a boat lies in a trench with her stem to the south. The old lord is in her on a bed, with bowls and hooped buckets round him. The turf is stacked ready.
I have the burial verse made. There is a place in it, between the horse and the bed, for a stranger's gift, if a stranger has one. If not, I have a line about the weather.
You have glass. I can hear it in how your men carry the crate.
Promise her glass by next harvest
Set a glass cup at the old lord's hand, as a gift
Sell her the glass, and name a price
Stand with the household, and say nothing of trade
The winter nights

The ships are in the boat-house and the young men are home. Tonight is the first of the winter nights. The foot of the great stone is dark and wet, the ground round it trodden, and the hall is full to the door.

Night outside a turf-roofed hall: a grey stone taller than four men leaning like a mast, its foot dark and wet, trodden ground and torches; through the open door a crowded bench, a horn being passed hand to hand toward a man with a cross on a thong.
A merchant at the winter nights. Good. You bring news and no opinions about verse. Sit below the steersman and above the dogs.
Praise the summer when the ship is in the boat-house. She is in. Drink. Whoever goes dry in my hall tonight insults the year.
A horn is coming down the bench toward you, and after it a bowl. Your own men are watching what you will do with each.
Snow at midsummer, and the corn black in the ear. We keep the feast all the same. A year you do not greet will not greet you.
Drink the horn, say a good word for the year, and pass the bowl on
Send to the boat for a cask of wine for the hall
Thank the hall, and keep the night aboard with your own
Four on one stick
A thin dark man in a red cloak too good for him sits near the high seat turning an arm ring while he thinks. A rune-cut stick is thrust in his belt. He sees you before you see him.

A hall bench by the long fire: a thin dark poet with a trimmed beard and a red cloak too fine for him turns an arm ring on his wrist, a rune-cut stick in his belt; shields and a striped sail hang behind the high seat.
A merchant. Good. Merchants have news and no opinions about verse. Sit. What has happened in the world?
My Frisian. I made a line about your boat. It is short, like the boat. You may not like it.
Four questions on one stick, eight pennies' weight. The answers are free, if you can find them.
Or pay me in a story from the south that I have not heard. A true one if you must.
Thor wades this water every day on his way to the ash. That is why the fishing is bad on judgement days.
The poet of the Danes' hall has one good line. I have heard it. It is mine. He will tell you the same of me, and he will be lying.
That is our smith. You have him lamed by the wrong king, and you have left out the best of the revenge. But you have him. A Frisian with Weland in his chest.
Buy the stick (8 d)
Tell him the English lay of the smith Weland, as far as you have it
Tell him what has happened in the world
The second ship
North of the strand a long low boat-house of turf and stone opens straight on the water, and beside it a hull stands half built under the sky. A lean man sights along a strake and says nothing.

A turf-and-stone boat-house opening on a grey sound, a hull on rollers inside and another half built beside it: a lean wright with grey-fair hair tied back with yarn, an adze on his shoulder and a knotted cord round his neck sights along a strake; a trough steaming.
Frisian boat. Broad. Lapped well enough. Your third strake on the steering side is weeping. No, the other third.
She still leaks where I said. You have not fixed it. You have put moss in it. That is not fixing.
There is no oak on this island. A ship comes here as trees in another ship. People forget that when they ask the price.
The chief wants twenty benches. He has silver for twelve. I have told him. He says build the twenty.
I am fitting new rowlocks to a boat I built fourteen winters ago. Do not ask what for. Everybody knows.
I owe the smith in the Vik for rivets, a winter overdue. If you see him, tell him the chief has not paid me either. He will understand. He hilts for the same man.
Sell him two loads of oak
Take his order for straight oak
Have him fix the weeping strake properly (8 d)
Bail her
The woman at the stone
Beside the hall a grey stone taller than four men leans a little, like a mast in a swell. A woman with a staff sits on the lesser of the two mounds beside it, looking at the sound and not at you.

A grey standing stone taller than four men leaning beside a turf-roofed hall, a mound on either side: on the lesser mound a weathered woman in a grey cloak with a staff shod in iron looks out over a narrow sound; children at the stone's foot who have been told not to climb.
You stand downwind of the stone like a man who was told not to climb it. Good. I am not the stone. I only sit by it.
The Frisian. The swell said a small boat. It did not say whose. It never gives names.
I read the swell. An old man on the strand reads it too and calls it knowing. I read it and call it seeing. We agree every morning, and it annoys us both.
The stone leans a finger more than when I was a girl. When it falls, they say, that is the end of things. I have told the children not to climb. They climb.
You have been to the lake in the Vik. I can see her look on you. She says I guess. She sits by flat water. Anyone can see in flat water.
Ask her about the crossing (3 d)
Offer to carry her answer back to the woman at the lake
Stand a while by the stone, and say nothing
The striped sail
A plump man in a scarlet cloak comes down the shingle in new shoes, with armed men behind him. He stops where he can see into your hold, and smiles.

A shingle beach at morning: a plump man in a scarlet cloak with a silver clasp and rings on both hands points at sacks in the hold of a merchant boat, armed men behind him; further up the strand an old patched sail lies on the stones beside a ship stripped of her fine striped one.
Good morning. Who commands this ship, and what is her errand? Take your time. I have all day, and the king's seal.
The king forbids corn, malt and meal to go north. I did not make the law. I only see that it is kept. What is under the hides?
Further up the strand a northern ship lies stripped: twenty men, no corn, and an old patched sail where a striped one hung.
A northern man came for corn and bought it from thralls. I took the corn, and his sail was better than mine. When we took the sail from him he wept.
That is a good sail you have.
Give up the corn to the king's stacks, and keep your sail by a gift to the bailiff (24 d)
Say the sacks are salt, and slip the sound at night
Turn south again with your corn, and sell it where the law allows
At Ripa no Frisian has brought Rhenish pots since the ice went. A woman offered two ounces of silver for one with a crack in it.
King Cnut was at Rome at Easter and won from the emperor that his merchants and pilgrims should go and come without unjust tolls on the road.
Men of the fleets are home at the Slie from England with more pennies than they can spend. Wine, glass and fine cloth sell there in autumn for what is asked.
At Ahus the comb-makers are at home from the winter nights to the first day of summer, and pay then for shed antler by the bundle.
They say at the Vik's market that Thorleif of the Karmsund is drowned off the Stad, ship and all, and that his widow sells his swords and tusks cheap.
